title: Architectural Allostatic Overloading: Exploring a Connection between Architectural Form and Allostatic Overloading
review_question: To conceptually understand the relationship between stress-inducing architectural features and allostatic loads, and to outline how neuroarchitectural researchers might empirically measure architecturally mediated allostatic overload in the future.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not formally specified; based on an interdisciplinary desk review of literature from neuroimmunology and neuroarchitecture.

findings.antecedent: Certain architectural forms (room proportions, wall curvature, window arrangement and size)
findings.quote: exposure to certain architectural forms... regularly provoke stress responses in humans without their conscious perception.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design (integrating live organic material) and biomorphic design (imitating organic contours/motifs)
findings.quote: biophilic design has a restorative effect... eliciting 'stress-reducing' responses within the body

findings.antecedent: Chronic exposure to stress-inducing architectural forms
findings.quote: chronic exposure to stress-inducing architectural forms may contribute to allostatic overloading

findings.antecedent: Urban environmental stressors (lead exposure, pollution perception, pollution, dangerous traffic, household crowding, environmental riskscapes, poor indoor environmental quality)
findings.quote: factors such as lead exposure... and poor indoor environmental quality... are all associated with a higher allostatic load.

findings.antecedent: Poor perceived neighborhood quality (overall condition of residential units, recreational space, perceived disorder/deterioration)
findings.quote: perceived neighbourhood quality... has the potential to affect allostatic load

findings.antecedent: Greater tree cover within 500m of residence
findings.quote: Greater tree cover within 500 m of residence was also linked with lower allostatic load

findings.antecedent: Biomarkers used in neuroarchitecture studies (e.g., heart rate, HRV, salivary cortisol, EEG, GSR, fMRI) vs. Biomarkers used in allostatic load studies (e.g., urinary cortisol, epinephrine, norepinephrine, DHEA, blood pressure, HDL, HbA1c, cholesterol, BMI, WHR, CRP, IL-6, fibrinogen)
findings.consequent: Measurement of stress responses / allostatic load
findings.quote: the clinical biomarkers used in those studies differ substantially from those used to measure allostatic load.

synthesis_conclusions: Chronic exposure to stress-inducing architectural forms may contribute to allostatic overloading and systemic inflammation.

While architectural forms can elicit acute stress responses, the biomarkers used in neuroarchitecture studies differ from those used to measure allostatic load, making it inconclusive whether these acute responses lead to allostatic overload.

Further longitudinal public health studies are needed to investigate the relationship between specific architectural forms and allostatic load using appropriate clinical biomarkers and clinimetric approaches.
evidence_gaps: Lack of studies on the relationship between stress-inducing architectural features and allostatic load.
Discrepancy in biomarkers used for acute stress responses in neuroarchitecture vs. allostatic load.
Need for longitudinal studies to assess architecturally mediated allostatic overload.
Need for studies incorporating clinimetric approaches to contextualize physiological responses to architectural forms.
heterogeneity_sources: Variability in responses to stress across populations (e.g., age, centenarians' conservative stress response mechanism).
Preexisting conditions (e.g., high blood pressure, diabetes) complicating stress responses.
External factors (age, biological sex, socioeconomic deprivation) influencing allostatic load measurement outcomes.

moderators.effect: Decline in stress response efficacy with age contributes to age-related diseases, but some individuals (centenarians) develop conservative stress response mechanisms. Also influences allostatic load measurement outcomes.
Complicates stress responses (e.g., high blood pressure, diabetes).
May play a role in influencing an individual's response to stress.

limitations: Lack of consensus on standardized measurement methods for allostatic load (biomarkers, combinations, clinimetric techniques).
Limited scope of biomarkers, potentially not capturing the entirety of physiological responses to stress.
Variability in responses to stress across populations.
Influence of external factors (age, biological sex, socioeconomic deprivation) on allostatic load, making it difficult to isolate specific factors.
Cross-sectional nature of most allostatic load studies to date (though longitudinal studies are emerging).
Difficulty in isolating spatial features from external factors in neuroarchitecture research.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This paper examines, conceptually, the relationship between stress-inducing architectural features and allostatic overload by drawing on literature from neuroimmunology and neuroarchitecture. The studies reviewed from the field of neuroimmunology indicate that chronic or repeated exposure to stress-inducing events may overwhelm the body’s regulatory system, resulting in a process termed allostatic overload. While there is evidence from the field of neuroarchitecture that short-term exposure to particular architectural features produce acute stress responses, there is yet to be a study on the relationship between stress-inducing architectural features and allostatic load. This paper considers how to design such a study by reviewing the two primary methods used to measure allostatic overload: biomarkers and clinimetrics. Of particular interest is the observation that the clinical biomarkers used to measure stress in neuroarchitectural studies differ substantially from those used to measure allostatic load. Therefore, the paper concludes that while the observed stress responses to particular architectural forms may indicate allostatic activity, further research is needed to determine whether these stress responses are leading to allostatic overload. Consequently, a discrete longitudinal public health study is advised, one which engages the clinical biomarkers indicative of allostatic activity and incorporates contextual data using a clinimetric approach.
